new_statements.rule_in_words: Wojokeso/Ampale has a lexically contrastive pitch accent, realized as high pitch plus stress (and some vowel lengthening). Its position is not predictable by rule but is confined to a two-syllable window: it falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable of a grammatical root; within the phonological word (root plus clitics/affixes, compounds) it can therefore surface anywhere. Accent on any other stem syllable signals a compound (Lloyd & West 1969 ms). Tonal perturbation between morphemes is regressive. The SIL OPD (West 1992) restates the system as two phonemic tones (high/low) with 'contrastive pitch accent'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: pitch accent on a syllable other than the last two of a stem indicates a compound; in compounds of two low roots the final syllable of the first root acquires pitch accent by regressive perturbation (Lloyd & West 1969 ms, p.1-2). Centralized high vowels never bear pitch accent (West 1992 OPD).
new_statements.domain_note: Accent is a property of the grammatical root (last two syllables); the 'phonological word' including affixes/clitics is the domain within which it may surface anywhere. Statements are about lexical words/stems, not phrase-level prominence. Lloyd's sketch is explicitly second-hand from West & West's then-forthcoming phonology (published as Cochran, Weimer & West 1981), but is itself a published primary-literature description by an Angan specialist.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the northern dialect, Wojokeso (= Wajokeso, Woyokeso; Imani/Imane village area), of the Ampale/Ampeeli language, which Glottolog files under Safeyoka safe1240 / ISO apz (no separate dialect glottocode known). Lloyd 1973 explicitly says the analysis follows West & West's Wojokeso work; his examples exclude the Aiwomba (central) dialect phoneme /ž/.

sources.note: p.1 (scanned): 'When pitch accent occurs on syllables other than the last or second to last of the stem, it is suspected that these words are compounds.' Normal noun-stem pitch patterns are final /\ and \\; in low+low compounds 'the final syllable of the first root gains pitch accent as a result of regressive perturbation.' Uses 'pitch accent', not 'stress'.
